title: The night of the senses
hook: when prayer stops feeling good, God may be weaning us from the sweets

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: a love poem, a sleeping house, a soul slipping out to meet God. Your line was my house being now at rest. Did you sit a minute in the dark? Today, John explains the first part of that night. Day two hundred sixty-one.

Here's something people who pray don't always say out loud. At the start, it can feel wonderful. Mass, a quiet church, a psalm read slowly, and something warm comes. Tears, sometimes. Peace. Going back is easy. And then one day, it's just gone. Show up, say the words. Nothing. Flat as cardboard. It's easy to conclude that something went wrong, or that God has left, or that it was never real. John of the Cross had a very different explanation.
screen: `AT FIRST, IT FEELS WONDERFUL.` → `THEN ONE DAY, NOTHING.` → `DID GOD LEAVE?`

segments.voice: First, the mother. John opens his book the Dark Night with a homely picture. A loving mother holds her baby close, warms it, and feeds it with sweet milk. That's how God treats beginners in prayer, he says: with comfort and sweetness. Second, the weaning. But a mother who loves her child doesn't nurse it forever. The day comes when she weans it. She sets it down so it will learn to walk, and it cries, because it wants the milk. Saint Paul says something similar to one young church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet." John says God does the same with souls. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so they can grow. Third, the sweet tooth. John is funny and sharp about beginners. He lists their faults in prayer: wanting more and more good feelings, like a spiritual sweet tooth; judging others who seem less devout; getting sulky when prayer is dull. The night of the senses, he says, is God's cure for all that. When the feelings dry up, you find out whether you were seeking God, or the sweets God gave. Fourth, dry is not gone. That's the heart of it. Dryness in prayer, John says, can be a sign that God is closer, not farther. It's God doing the work now, quietly, below what you can feel. He doesn't say every dry spell is this. Tomorrow he'll give us ways to tell. But he says: don't assume God left because the sweetness did.
screen: `A MOTHER FEEDS HER BABY MILK.` · `THEN SHE WEANS IT TO WALK.` · `A SPIRITUAL SWEET TOOTH.` · `DRY IS NOT GONE.` · then, large: `I GAVE YOU MILK TO DRINK, NOT MEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray today even if it's dry. Sit, and breathe. Don't try to make anything happen. If you pray, just be with God for these two minutes, even if it feels like talking to a wall. That counts. If you don't pray, sit with something you've been faithful to that doesn't feel exciting anymore, a friendship, a job, a promise, and notice that showing up still matters. The bell holds the time.
Sweetness. The comfort God gives beginners in prayer, which the night of the senses takes away, the way a mother weans a child, so the soul can grow. Today's word.
Your line: dry is not gone. Today, do one faithful thing that doesn't feel like anything, and do it anyway. Day two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors often turn to John's Dark Night, book one, when people say prayer has gone dry, and encourage them to keep praying faithfully rather than chasing feelings.

fork.setup: you've prayed every day for a year, and it used to feel wonderful. now it feels like nothing. what does John say?
options: you've done something wrong; stop until you find it.
God may be weaning you from the sweets; keep going.
fork.reveal: John says God takes the sweetness away so the soul can grow, the way a mother weans a child. dry is not gone.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy phrase for losing your faith.
what it means: a season when prayer stops feeling good, as God weans the soul from sweetness toward a deeper love.
what a scholar hears: Dark Night, book one: the nursing mother (1.1), the beginners' faults under the seven capital sins (1.2–7), and the passive night of sense (1.8).

sources.quoted: I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet.

sources.work: John of the Cross, The Dark Night

notes: The nursing mother who weans her child (Dark Night 1.1.2) and the beginners' imperfections under the seven capital sins, including 'spiritual gluttony' (1.2–7), paraphrased. 'Spiritual sweet tooth' is our gloss on spiritual gluttony. Confirm.
1 Corinthians 3:2 is offered as a parallel; John does cite Paul's milk and solid food image in his works, but confirm whether in this chapter.
The script notes that not every dry spell is the dark night, pointing to tomorrow's three signs.

Editor review (2026-10-01): moved the hook out of second person so it no longer tells the listener what they feel, and cut 'most people assume'; cut 'a picture everyone knows'; changed 'dryness is often a sign God is closer' to 'can be a sign' (teach, match, myth), to match the script's own caution that not every dry spell is this night.
